paragraphs.heading: Magnetic memories in rock
paragraphs.text: Paleomagnetism studies Earth's magnetic field in prehistoric times, as recorded in rocks, sediment and archaeological objects. Some magnetic minerals capture the direction and strength of the field at the moment they form. That record shows how the field behaved and where tectonic plates used to be. The sequence of field flips stored in layers of volcanic and sedimentary rock, called magnetostratigraphy, also serves as a tool for dating.

paragraphs.heading: Early observations
paragraphs.text: By the 1700s people had noticed compass needles swinging off course near strongly magnetized rock outcrops. In 1797 Alexander von Humboldt blamed lightning strikes, which do often magnetize surface rocks. In the 1800s, studies found some recent lavas magnetized in line with Earth's field, and early in the 1900s Brunhes and others showed that many rocks were magnetized the opposite way. In the late 1920s Motonori Matuyama showed the field had flipped in the mid-Quaternary, an event now called the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal.

paragraphs.heading: Proving the continents move
paragraphs.text: Alfred Wegener argued in 1915 that the continents were once joined and had since moved apart. Few accepted it, because no one knew what drove the motion or how to trace the continents' paths through time. In 1956 Blackett invented a sensitive astatic magnetometer, which became the basic tool of paleomagnetism. Irving drew apparent polar wander paths for Europe and North America; the two curves split apart but could be matched if the continents had touched until 200 million years ago. This was the first clear geophysical evidence for continental drift, and in 1963 Morley, Vine and Matthews showed that magnetic anomalies in the sea floor backed up seafloor spreading.

paragraphs.heading: Locking in the field as rock cools
paragraphs.text: In basalt and other igneous rocks, iron-titanium oxide minerals can hold onto the direction of the field as they cool through their Curie temperatures. For magnetite that point is about 580 °C, while most basalt and gabbro have fully crystallized below 900 °C. So the grains are not physically turned to face the field; instead they record which way it points. This record is called thermoremanent magnetization, or TRM. It is not always accurate or lasting, but in the basalts of ocean crust it survived well enough to be critical to theories of sea floor spreading.

paragraphs.heading: Fire leaves a magnetic mark
paragraphs.text: TRM also forms in pottery kilns, hearths and burned adobe buildings. Studying it in such archaeological materials is the basis of archaeomagnetic dating. The Māori of New Zealand made no pottery, but their steam ovens, called hāngī, which are 700 to 800 years old, still provide enough material for this work.

paragraphs.heading: Sediments and new minerals
paragraphs.text: Sediments record the field by a different route. Magnetic grains can line up with the field while they settle or soon after, which is called detrital remanent magnetization. A third way works through chemistry: new magnetic grains form in reactions and capture the field's direction at the time they appear, known as chemical remanent magnetization, or CRM. Hematite, an iron oxide that forms when other minerals in the rock such as magnetite oxidize, commonly carries this kind of record.
